item.title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs
item.description: arXiv:2610.22377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Busemann (Osnabr\"uck University, CLAAS E-Systems GmbH), Torben T\"oniges (CLAAS E-Systems GmbH), Martin Atzmueller (Semantic Information Systems Group, Osnabr\"uck University, German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence)

item.title: MemLLM: End-to-end In-Storage Acceleration of On-device Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Precomputed KV Caches
item.description: arXiv:2610.22579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices enables personalized large language model (LLM) inference while preserving privacy. However, RAG's inherent length asymmetry makes the prefill phase the dominant bottleneck. While precomputing the KV caches offline alleviates the prefill cost on server systems, the multi-gigabyte caches over the narrow interconnect create a severe I/O wall for on-device systems. To mitigate this, we propose MemLLM, an end-to-end in-storage processing (ISP) architecture that executes the complete attention pipeline based on precomputed KV caches within the SSD. MemLLM utilizes per-channel accelerators to fully utilize the aggregated NAND channel bandwidth and accelerates all KV cache-related computations on the storage-side to minimize PCIe transfers. To efficiently handle the sparse updates required by RAG, MemLLM introduces a fused recomputation-query kernel paired with a hardware-based filter logic to halve the NAND read volume and eliminate write-back penalties. Furthermore, MemLLM's global SRAM-based stateful reduction engine enables a completely DRAM-less dataflow, thereby removing the internal memory bottlenecks and bounding the PCIe egress to an $O(1)$ footprint. A full-stack software stack allows asynchronous, zero-copy transfers from the ISP to the host and provides transparent execution within modern ML frameworks. Evaluated across eight real-world RAG datasets and six on-device LLM models, MemLLM achieves an average end-to-end speedup of 4.06$\times$ over the GPU baseline.
item.dc:creator: Seungkwan Kang, Hyungseok Ko, Heemin Kim, Myoungsoo Jung

item.title: CMM-MP: A Novel Memory Pooling Architecture using Purpose-built Memory Device with CXL and Ethernet
item.description: arXiv:2610.22716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CXL Memory Module - Memory Pooling (CMM-MP) introduces a novel memory pooling architecture to meet the unique requirements of emerging memory-intensive workloads. This industry-first, purpose-built memory-pooling device combines the benefits of Compute Express Link (CXL) with the scalability and cost advantages of Ethernet. Multiple CMM-MP devices together provide a flexible, composable, and disaggregated memory expansion solution. The CMM-MP enables 100s of TB capacity for GPU/CPU applications without modifications. The memory pool is exposed as a large-capacity logical aggregate memory, with all pool discovery, composition, and backend network datapath tasks fully offloaded to the device. CMM-MP supports both memory pooling and sharing usage modes. It provides an application latency of 2.7 us and up to 23 GB/s of memory throughput. Our evaluations demonstrate that CMM-MP significantly outperforms RDMA-based solutions in latency and throughput. We also evaluated real-world use cases of Valkey+YCSB and DiskANN using CMM-MP.
item.dc:creator: Michael Wasef, Gongjin Sun, Edmund Au, Ranjitha Gopalakrishna, Elham Movahedian, Dongyang Li, Senthil Murugesapandian, Caroline Kahn, Shuyu Lyu, Brian Luu, Jason Scott, Namita Kumar, Mehdi Nik, Kwan Huen, Xuebin Yao, Amir Beygi, Luis Vitorio Cargnini, Ramdas Kachare

item.title: BS-Spec: BFP-Based Bit-Sharing for Self-Speculative LLM Decoding with LUT-Driven Mixed-Precision Acceleration
item.description: arXiv:2610.22877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse inference services, serving workloads span a wide range of batch sizes, context lengths, and performance requirements. Speculative decoding improves inference throughput, but conventional approaches require a separate draft model and KV cache, while existing self-speculative methods suffer from workload-insensitive draft configurations and inefficient mixed-precision execution. In this paper, we present BS-Spec, a block floating point (BFP)-based bit-sharing framework that jointly optimizes draft construction, workload-aware precision selection, and hardware execution. BS-Spec derives multiple draft representations directly from a single BFP target model by partially loading the most significant bits of weights and the KV cache while preserving shared exponents, eliminating separate draft-model storage. Offline calibration selects the weight and KV-cache precision pair that maximizes estimated speedup for each serving regime, and a precision lookup table applies the selected configuration at runtime. To support this adaptive execution, we design a mixed-precision BFP accelerator with a lookup table (LUT)-based variable-precision datapath for both draft and target computation. Experimental results show that BS-Spec achieves up to $1.9\times$ speedup over conventional autoregressive decoding and improves speedup over the evaluated bit-sharing self-speculative decoding baselines by $67.2\%$ on average, demonstrating the benefits of jointly co-designing bit sharing, precision adaptation, and specialized hardware for diverse LLM serving workloads.
item.dc:creator: Jiwoo Kim, Gunho Park, Sunwoo Yoo, Baeseong Park, Dongsoo Lee, Youngjoo Lee

item.title: qGAMMA: A Framework for Optimal DNN Mapping on Multi-Precision Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2610.23222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work describes qGAMMA, a flexible framework for exploring and optimizing the mapping of mixed-precision Deep Neural Network (DNN) models onto general-purpose spatial accelerators that support a range of fixed- and floating-point precisions. qGAMMA navigates the design space using a domain-specific genetic algorithm and an analytical performance model based on hardware synthesis results. The framework identifies the optimal mapping and accelerator configuration that minimizes target metrics. Extensive evaluations across DNN workloads show that qGAMMA offers valuable insights for designing mixed-precision applications, enabling better trade-offs between performance, energy efficiency, and resource utilization.
item.dc:creator: Leandro Fiorin, Luigi Altamura, Cristina Silvano

item.title: GUMPIM: Unitary and Malleable Memory for Processing-in-Memory with Guaranteed PIM Pages
item.description: arXiv:2610.23406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DRAM-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) addresses the "memory wall" by executing computations directly inside main memory. However, memory interleaving and virtual memory limit contiguous data size visible to PIM units, constraining PIM task granularity. To mitigate this, existing PIM systems drastically isolate PIM memory or disable memory interleaving. These design choices, however, decrease the CPU memory bandwidth and introduce extra data transfer, leading to an additional "system memory wall" that must be resolved to realize PIM's full potential. In this work, we propose GUMPIM, a PIM system that allows interleaved CPU pages and non-interleaved PIM pages to coexist in a Unitary and Malleable memory space with Guaranteed PIM page allocation. GUMPIM enables zero-copy during PIM task offloading and maintains CPU memory bandwidth while ensuring low PIM offloading overhead. First, we propose a dual-track memory management mechanism consisting of independent page allocation and address translation for CPU and PIM pages. Second, we design GUMPIM interface hardware on PIM-enabled DRAMs to provide a dynamic address mapping for the different data layouts of CPU and PIM pages. Third, we propose a PIM-assisted page migration mechanism that transparently migrates pages while preserving CPU access bandwidth, thereby enabling guaranteed and accelerated PIM page allocation. GUMPIM requires no changes to commodity DRAM standards; all hardware modifications are limited to the DRAM side, ensuring full compatibility with existing CPUs and enabling immediate deployment on current HBMx- and LPDDRx-based PIM platforms. Our results show only <0.1% performance degradation for CPU workloads on GUMPIM. For PIM workloads, GUMPIM reduces memory allocation and CPU-part computation times by 2.7x and 4.93x, respectively, yielding an end-to-end 2.3x speedup over a state-of-the-art baseline system.

item.title: HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0--19.0$\times$ faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.
item.dc:creator: Jinheng Li, Guosheng Wang, Hongchao Du, Shangyu Wu, Qiao Li, Chun Jason Xue

item.title: Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains
item.description: arXiv:2610.23724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design space of modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures, including GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators; memory tech- nologies, including HBM, GDDR, and SRAM; and interconnects such as NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet. No single architecture is optimal across LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC workloads, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present ArchAgent, a hierarchical multi- agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems, each handled by specialist agents. A deterministic analytical evaluator closes the loop, ensuring that all performance estimates are derived from analytical models rather than generated by the LLM. On a mixed AI+HPC workload under a 1 MW power budget, ArchAgent discovers heterogeneous designs that achieve a 1.93x weighted geometric mean speedup over a homogeneous GPU baseline, while requiring only 18 evaluations compared with 100 evaluations for hill climbing, which achieves 1.65x speedup.
item.dc:creator: Murali Emani, Kashyap R Manjusha

item.title: TileDRAM: Compiler-Controlled Tile-to-DRAM Layouts for 3D DRAM GPGPUs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern GPU compilers expose rich layout abstractions for mapping tensors to threads and on-chip resources, but compute-unit-local (CU-local) 3D DRAM architectures lack a corresponding abstraction for specifying how operand-tile data are arranged within the DRAM address space. Without such an abstraction, conventional placement under the existing DRAM address mapping can subject structured tile accesses to severe row-buffer conflicts. We present TileDRAM, a compiler-runtime toolchain that introduces tile-to-DRAM layouts as a compiler-visible abstraction for DRAM placement. TileDRAM extends the GPU Linear Layout abstraction from compute-side mapping targets to DRAM placement coordinates and selects layouts per tile access signature, using recurring tile-local access behavior as the specialization unit. Since row-buffer locality depends on ordered request history, TileDRAM evaluates candidate layouts through their row-buffer behavior under fixed DRAM address mappings. Accesses under the selected layouts are realized through ordinary address arithmetic, without new address-remapping hardware or ISA support. In full-trace replay on Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 across 108 mixture-of-experts (MoE) feed-forward network (FFN) cases, TileDRAM reduces the request-weighted row-conflict rate from 75.7% to 15.2% and achieves a 1.77x geomean speedup. Retargeting six traces to six 3D DRAM organizations yields a 2.20x geomean speedup under the same compiler abstraction. On an RTX 3090, address transformation adds 0.17% geomean overhead over identity.
item.dc:creator: Guangyuan Xu, Lanxuan Zhang, Ziyang Li, Zhaoshi Li, Yajun Ha

item.title: Understanding LLM Hallucinations Caused by Soft Errors
item.description: arXiv:2610.22520v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively studied from a software perspective, limited attention has been paid to hardware-level factors. In this paper, we performed a case study to understand LLM hallucination caused by soft errors on hardware. We introduce LLMEI to inject soft errors into LLMs during inference, based on what we evaluate the impact of soft error across diverse LLM architectures and tasks, including mathematical reasoning and code generation. We summarize the taxonomy of different failure modes based on LLM hallucination behaviors and analyze their distributions under different error rates. Our find- ings underscore the hallucination-specific diagnostics within the reliability of LLM implementation on hardware.
item.dc:creator: Jinghao Wen, Dongning Ma, Ruixuan Wang, Shaohuang Wang, Xun Jiao

item.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2610.22811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
item.dc:creator: Se Un Park, Kyungkeon Chung, Huigeol Kim, Junyoung Park

item.title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.23415v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.
item.dc:creator: Saim Rehman, Muhammad Shafique

item.title: Veri-Sure: Multi-Agent RTL Code Generation with Temporal Tracing, Slicing and Formal Verification
item.description: arXiv:2601.19747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the rapidly evolving field of Electronic Design Automation (EDA), the deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) for Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation has emerged as a promising direction. However, because RTL code describes concurrent hardware behavior with strict cycle-level timing and thus differs fundamentally from software code, LLM-based RTL code generation remains bottlenecked by (i) sparse feedback and limited test coverage of simulation-centric evaluation, (ii) regressions and repair hallucinations introduced by whole-file regeneration during debugging, and (iii) semantic drift as intent is reinterpreted across repair iterations and agent handoffs. In this work, we propose Veri-Sure, a multi-agent framework that establishes a design contract to align agents' intent and uses a patching mechanism guided by static dependency slicing to perform precise, localized repairs. By integrating a multi-branch verification pipeline that combines trace-driven temporal analysis with formal verification, Veri-Sure yields more robust and reliable RTL code generation. We also introduce VerilogEval-v2-EXT, extending the original benchmark with 53 more industrial-grade design tasks and stratified difficulty levels, and show that Veri-Sure achieves state-of-the-art verified-correct RTL code generation performance, surpassing standalone LLMs and prior agentic systems. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/xyjoey/Veri-Sure.
item.dc:creator: Jiale Liu, Taiyu Zhou, Tianqi Jiang

item.title: Is Your NPU Ready for LLMs? Dissecting the Hidden Efficiency Bottlenecks in Mobile LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2607.05475v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) on mobile devices enhances privacy and reduces latency, but is severely constrained by hardware inefficiencies. We present the first comprehensive, cross-layer measurement study of mobile LLM inference, spanning five mainstream frameworks (e.g., llama.cpp and GENIE) and three hardware backends (CPU, GPU, and NPU). To enable this analysis, we develop PowerBench, a fine-grained profiling tool that measures LLM throughput and provides the first backend-specific energy attribution for mobile LLM inference, going beyond traditional device-level measurements. We further conduct hardware microbenchmarks to characterize the memory-system performance and compute capabilities of mobile CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. Our study yields three critical insights: (1) Framework-induced performance gaps are substantially amplified on NPUs, reaching up to $10\times$ due to differences in offloading strategies, hardware-underutilizing operators, and activation quantization strategies. (2) We identify a distinct ``phase split,'' in which NPUs excel at compute-bound prefilling, while CPUs outperform all other backends in memory-bound decoding. This split is driven by NPUs' preference for large, fixed-shape workloads, which conflicts with the small-kernel, dynamic nature of decoding. (3) Backend-specific profiling uncovers substantial scheduling headroom missed by prior work. Suboptimal thread configurations, uncoordinated NPU sleep latencies, and CPU polling intervals result in unnecessary energy consumption. For example, tuning CPU frequency alone reduces energy consumption by up to $39.7\%$. Leveraging these findings, we estimate that an energy-oriented configuration can reduce energy consumption by up to $53.2\%$ on the NPU backend across three datasets, highlighting the substantial potential for further efficiency improvements in mobile LLM deployment.
item.dc:creator: Guanyu Cai, Ruiming Tian, Lang Yang, Zhouhong Ren, Jinliang Yuan, Lingkun Li, Jiliang Wang

item.title: Rethinking Agentic Kernel Generation for Emerging Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2608.00894v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emerging accelerators often lack mature compiler backends, motivating neural agents that generate and repair kernels from architectural documentation and simulator feedback. This approach repeatedly reconstructs workload-invariant machine semantics, including instruction behavior, legality constraints, synchronization rules, and memory protocols, for every workload. We argue that these semantics should be compiled once into a persistent symbolic artifact, while neural reasoning should focus on workload-dependent mapping decisions. We present Zomboss, a compiler-mediated agentic framework for kernel generation that places neural search within a verified compiler boundary. Zomboss compiles machine semantics and legality constraints into a reusable mapping interface, then uses a neural agent to optimize workload-dependent decisions within the validated mapping space. Across 20 Gemmini and 36 PLENA workload instances, Zomboss returns a correct verified kernel on all 56 instances. Relative to the compiler default, Zomboss achieves geometric-mean speedups of 3.34x on Gemmini and 1.10x on PLENA. Additional comparisons against KernelCraft reduce tokens per verified kernel by 26.3% on 20 Gemmini instances and 98.2% on 18 composite PLENA instances. These results show that partial mapping specification and symbolic completion turn kernel generation into verified design-space exploration. The shared interface supports competitive conventional and neural search, while improving kernel quality and token efficiency within the same agentic harness. Zomboss thus separates reusable machine realization from the policies that explore workload-dependent mappings.
item.dc:creator: Ruijie Gao, Jirong Yang, Barry Lyu, Haoran Jin, Nathan Bleier

item.title: A LoRa-Compatible Receiver with Programmable Noise-Power Trade-Off and Integrated Wake-Up Mode
item.description: arXiv:2610.20677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Programmable receivers allow an optimal performance in the variable conditions of the wireless channel. An extensive analysis of their noise-power trade-off enables the development of a main receiver with embedded wake-up circuitry. This makes the seamless integration of wake-up receivers (WuRXs) in RF receivers possible, avoiding power, area, complexity, and cost overheads in the system. In this paper, we propose the first LoRa-compatible receiver with an integrated wake-up mode and a programmable noise-power trade-off. In main-receiver mode, it consumes 4.57 mW for a sensitivity of -138 dBm, but it can save up to 62.6% of power consumption at the cost of an 8.3-dB sensitivity degradation. In wake-up mode, sensitivity down to -126 dBm is achieved for a 32-ms latency and 1.5 mW of power consumption. The power consumption remains relatively high due to a sub-optimal design of the the phase-locked loop (PLL). In the end, the wake-up mode consumes 3X less than the lowest-noise configuration in main-receiver mode.
item.dc:creator: Marco Gonzalez, Pol Maistriaux, J\'er\^ome Louveaux, David Bol

item.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2511.23440v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning models perform well across domains such as diagnostics, weather forecasting, NLP, and autonomous driving, but their limited uncertainty handling restricts use in safety-critical settings. Traditional neural networks often fail to detect out-of-domain (OOD) data and may output confident yet incorrect predictions. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by providing probabilistic estimates, but incur high computational cost because predictions require sampling weight distributions and multiple forward passes. The Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) offers a highly efficient approximation to Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) by assuming Gaussian-distributed weights and activations, enabling fully analytic uncertainty propagation and replacing sampling with a single deterministic forward pass. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compiling, optimizing, and deploying PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. Using the TVM deep learning compiler, we implement a dedicated library of Gaussian-propagating operators for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks, combined with manual and automated tuning strategies. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency, achieving speedups of up to 4200x for small mini-batches. PFP-BNNs match SVI-BNNs on Dirty-MNIST in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and OOD detection while greatly reducing compute cost. These results highlight the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation to enable efficient BNN deployment on resource-constrained systems.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard Klein, Falk Selker, Hendrik Borras, Sophie Steger, Franz Pernkopf, Holger Fr\"oning

item.title: Machine Learning on Heterogeneous, Edge, and Quantum Hardware for Particle Physics (ML-HEQUPP)
item.description: arXiv:2602.22248v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The next generation of particle physics experiments will face a new era of challenges in data acquisition, due to unprecedented data rates and volumes along with extreme environments and operational constraints. Harnessing this data for scientific discovery demands real-time inference and decision-making, intelligent data reduction, and efficient processing architectures beyond current capabilities. Crucial to the success of this experimental paradigm are several emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML), silicon microelectronics, and the advent of quantum algorithms and processing. Their intersection includes areas of research such as low-power and low-latency devices for edge computing, heterogeneous accelerator systems, reconfigurable hardware, novel codesign and synthesis strategies, readout for cryogenic or high-radiation environments, and analog computing. This white paper presents a community-driven vision to identify and prioritize research and development opportunities in hardware-based ML systems and corresponding physics applications, contributing towards a successful transition to the new data frontier of fundamental science.
